column2: A dramatic genre of humorously confusing, sometimes ridiculous situations that ends happily, often in one or more marriages.
A mode in which a work ends happily, justice is done, the ravages of time are arrested, and that which is lost is found.
A feature of drama in which the audience knows that the outcome of an action will be the opposite of that intended by a character.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter lines, broken into verse paragraphs by sense rather than stanza form.
A more straightforward form of expression, distinguished from verse, which is more compressed and shaped by metrical norms.
The stylistic level of words, including their degree of formality, chosen according to audience and situation, from high style to informal or colloquial low style.
A dramatic topos in which a character, alone or thinking to be alone on stage, speaks so as to give the audience access to his or her private thoughts.
A figure of thought that identifies, or implicitly identifies, one thing with another with which it is not literally identifiable.
A figure of thought that compares one thing with another, usually using "like" or "as."
A figure of thought that attributes human qualities to nonhuman forces or objects.
A passing but illuminating reference within a literary text to another, well-known text, often biblical or classical.
A figure of thought in which a single word or expression has a sometimes irresolvable doubleness of meaning.
Two consecutive rhyming lines that usually contain the same number of stresses.
A play designed to provoke laughter through the often humiliating antics of stock characters.
The point at which a narrative can be resolved and so ended.
The moment of a protagonist's recognition in a narrative, which is also often the moment of moral understanding.
